piezas.titulo: Cortical thinning and functional reorganization as well as related transcriptomic signatures during early motor recovery following acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Acute basal ganglia ischemic stroke (ABGIS) commonly causes severe motor impairment, yet early spatiotemporal patterns of cortical morphological alterations and functional reorganization alongside the spatially coupled transcriptomic signatures remain unclear. Methods Twenty-six ABGIS patients and thirty-three normal controls (NCs) received multimodal MRI and neurological examinations, and patients were reassessed at 1-month follow-up. Cortical morphological changes and brain functional reorganization were analyzed based on cortical thickness (CT) and functional connectivity (FC). We identified the most discriminative FC features based on machine learning (ML) classification and interpretability analyses, and investigated transcriptomic signatures associated with FC alterations via the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Results No differences in CT were found between baseline ABGIS patients (ABGIS_1) and NCs. Compared with ABGIS_1, follow-up patients (ABGIS_2) exhibited reduced CT in the left postcentral gyrus (PoCG.L), left superior parietal lobule (SPL.L), and left supramarginal gyrus (SMG.L). Compared with NCs, ABGIS_1 showed decreased FC from PoCG.L/SPL.L to sensorimotor cortex and occipital cortex. ABGIS_2 presented elevated FC relative to ABGIS_1 between PoCG.L and the right precentral gyrus (PreCG.R), and between SPL.L and the bilateral precentral gyrus as well as right superior occipital gyrus. Longitudinal increases in FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R were positively correlated with improvements in Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores. ML models coupled with interpretability analyses preliminarily demonstrated that FC between PoCG.L/SPL.L and PreCG.R made prominent contributions to classification. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that gene sets correlated with FC alterations were mainly enriched in neuronal synaptic structure and synaptic signaling, chromatin regulation, as well as DNA and RNA metabolism. Conclusions This study verifies progressive cortical thinning and adaptive functional reorganization during early motor recovery following ABGIS, with such brain functional alterations paralleling distinct transcriptomic signatures, providing neuropathological and spatial transcriptomic clues for interpreting early motor recovery.

piezas.titulo: How Has AI Impacted Code Obfuscation?
piezas.resumenOriginal: AI is changing how developers protect software and how attackers analyze it. As large language models (LLMs) become more capable of generating and interpreting obfuscated code, developers must reconsider how much protection obfuscation provides. What Code Obfuscation Actually Means Code obfuscation rewrites a program into a form that behaves identically yet resists human comprehension. Common techniques include identifier renaming, control-flow restructuring, and data encoding, all aimed at raising the cost of reverse engineering and deterring intellectual property theft.

piezas.titulo: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
piezas.resumenOriginal: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

piezas.titulo: Development of the Children's Occupational Justice Scale Across Metropolitan and Non-Metropolitan Contexts.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceOccupational justice is a core concept in occupational therapy; however, no standardized self-report measure exists for school-aged children, limiting the identification of occupational inequities and evaluation of participation-focused interventions.ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Children's Occupational Justice Scale (COJS) and examine its ability to distinguish between children from metropolitan and non-metropolitan contexts.DesignCross-sectional scale development and psychometric validation study.SettingSchools located in metropolitan and non-metropolitan regions of Türkiye.ParticipantsA total of 873 children ages 11 to 14 years participated. Independent samples were used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA; n = 428) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; n = 445). Test-retest reliability was assessed in 94 participants.Outcomes and MeasuresThe preliminary COJS was developed through literature review, expert evaluation, and pilot testing. Construct validity, reliability, and known-groups validity were examined.ResultsEFA supported a 23-item, four-factor structure explaining 68.47% of the variance. CFA demonstrated good model fit (Comparative Fit Index = .957, Tucker-Lewis Index = .949, Goodness-of-Fit Index = .918, Root Mean Square Error of Approximation = .054, Standardized Root Mean Square Residual = .047). Internal consistency was excellent (Cronbach's α = .94; McDonald's ω = .95), and test-retest reliability was strong (intraclass correlation coefficient = .91, 95% confidence interval [.87, .94]). Children in metropolitan regions reported significantly higher occupational justice scores than children in non-metropolitan regions (p < .001).Conclusions and RelevanceThe COJS demonstrated strong validity and reliability for assessing occupational justice among school-aged children. The scale may provide occupational therapy practitioners and researchers with a novel tool for identifying occupational inequities and evaluating children's perceptions of participation opportunities, inclusion, choice, and environmental support.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: Real-world patterns of documented cognitive evaluation and dementia diagnoses after ischemic stroke in the U. S.: a retrospective EHR study
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionPost-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a common, often manifesting within 3–6 months after stroke and is associated with reduced quality of life, functional decline, and an increased dementia risk. Despite the potential benefits of early identification, cognitive screening remains inconsistent and real-world cognitive screening practices following stroke are poorly characterized. This study examined the documented cognitive screening practices and their association with dementia diagnoses among U. S. stroke survivors using the TriNetX research network.MethodsThis retrospective descriptive study analyzed real world electronic health record data from adults with first-ever ischemic stroke in the TriNetX research network from December 8, 2024, to December 8, 2025. Cognitive evaluation was defined by using an inclusive code set, i.e., cognitive assessment/screening and occupational therapy/rehabilitation codes potentially including cognition, and a specific code set, i.e., restricted to cognitive assessment/screening codes. Descriptive analyses examined documented dementia and the sequence and intervals among index strokes, cognitive evaluation-related coding, and dementia documentation in the two code sets.ResultsAmong 102,226 eligible stroke survivors, inclusive and specific cognitive evaluation codes were documented in 23.96% and 0.59% of these cases, respectively. Documented dementia diagnoses were more frequent among patients with cognitive evaluation codes than those without (inclusive: 1.78% vs. 0.81%; specific: 5.69% vs. 1.03%). The mean time from stroke to cognitive evaluation was 38.5 days for inclusive codes and 109.7 days for specific codes. Cognitive evaluation preceded dementia documentation in 70.4% and 22.0% of the code sets, respectively, while dementia was documented on or before the cognitive evaluation in 29.6% and 77.6% of the time.DiscussionDocumented cognitive evaluation after stroke was infrequent and varied substantially by coding definition. Specific cognitive assessment/screening codes were recorded in fewer than 1% of eligible stroke survivors and frequently occurred on or after dementia diagnosis, suggesting confirmatory evaluation rather than routine screening. The higher frequencies of dementia diagnoses among patients with cognitive evaluation-related codes may reflect clinical selection, underlying cognitive concerns, healthcare utilization, or differential diagnostic ascertainment rather than routine screening. Further studies incorporating structured cognitive assessments at predefined intervals are needed to identify optimal strategies for detecting PSCI in this population.

piezas.titulo: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
piezas.resumenOriginal: Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028. But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns . This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs. Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized , “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation. The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead Key • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision • Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development • Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress 1. Alan Turing 1936 Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI. REALITY CHECK Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm. 2. I. J. Good 1965 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” 3. Backpropagation 1986 Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks. 4. Vernor Vinge 1993 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess. 5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky 1990s–2000s Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively. 6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010s Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities. 7. The race to self-improving AI 2020s Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it. 8. Reality check 2020s François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain. YOU ARE HERE 2026 AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion? THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES 1. The Intelligence Explosion AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control. 2. Danger Without Superintelligence The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control. 3. A Useful AI Future Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation , an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science. An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine. Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI. Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here. Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts. We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper , “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle. We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress. A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out , rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming. At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists. Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design) Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow. To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers . Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.” These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision. Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate. In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind. I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence . The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions. Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives. The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them. The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world. This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence. What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.” This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”

piezas.titulo: Acute high-intensity interval exercise in spinal cord injury: psychological benefits alongside cognitive and neurobiological responses
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionAcute high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) can lead to improvements in executive functions, but less is known on if, and through what mechanisms, this applies after spinal cord injury (SCI). In this randomized within-subject crossover study, the effects of acute HIIE on working memory, cognitive task-related regional cerebral blood flow, blood biomarkers and psychological responses were investigated.MethodsSixteen adults with chronic SCI [mean age 43.3 ± 10.6 years; 12 men; 9 with paraplegia (T2–T12) and 7 with tetraplegia (C5–C8); > 1-year post-injury] completed a passive rest and a HIIE condition (20 min of double-poling ergometry at 80% of peak power output). Working memory (n-back task) performance was assessed pre- and post- intervention (planned: 10 min; actual post-intervention delay: 16.1 ± 4.4 min) with simultaneous measurement of hemodynamics using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) over the prefrontal cortex and transcranial doppler ultrasonography of the middle cerebral artery. Blood biomarkers (lactate, cortisol and BDNF isoforms) and psychological responses (affect, physical and mental fatigue) were assessed at multiple time points.ResultsLinear mixed models revealed no significant interaction effects between time and condition for most outcomes, but lactate increased post-HIIE and psychological responses improved following HIIE compared to Rest.DiscussionThe single supervised HIIE bout was well-tolerated in this screened SCI sample. It did not affect subsequent cognitive performance but was associated with transient improvements in affect (PANAS-SF) and mental fatigue. Adequately powered studies are needed to determine whether HIIE confers cognitive benefits in individuals with SCI and to clarify underlying mechanisms.

piezas.titulo: The neural basis of unfamiliar face recognition in humans with fMRI frequency-tagging
piezas.resumenOriginal: Faces provide the most diagnostic information for identifying individuals in humans. Understanding the neural mechanisms involved in face identity recognition (FIR) is particularly important for unfamiliar faces, for which identity cannot rely on encoded multimodal semantic associations. Here, we investigated the neural basis of FIR using an original frequency-tagging fMRI approach providing objective, sensitive, and reliable measures of face recognition. Ten human participants were presented within a rapid 6 Hz stream of natural images of a single unfamiliar identity in two conditions: (1) with the same face image across low-level changes (size, luminance, contrast) only, or (2) with images varying in background, size, head orientation, gaze direction, etc. Every 9 s during a 243 s run, seven images of different unfamiliar identities were introduced in bursts. For each participant and each condition, we recorded runs with upright and inverted faces. Analyses were performed within face-selective regions (defined from a frequency-tagging localizer) and in the Fourier domain, where individual face discrimination responses were objectively identified and quantified at the identity-change frequency (0.111 Hz). We observed robust image-based individual face discrimination responses across both conditions in core face-selective ventral regions (LatMidFG and IOG). In contrast, responses in early visual cortex and the pSTS were negligible in our second condition, which required generalization across viewpoint variations. In addition, the LatMidFG showed a reliable inversion effect, confirming that the observed responses cannot be attributed solely to low-level image differences. Overall, these findings highlight the value of fMRI frequency-tagging for objectively characterizing the cortical network underlying unfamiliar FIR, providing evidence for high-level discrimination and generalization of unfamiliar face identity in the human ventral occipito-temporal face-selective network.

piezas.titulo: A Standardized Occupational Therapy-Based Upper Extremity Assessment for Surgical Residency Onboarding.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Objective This initiative targets technical readiness and ergonomic awareness within surgical residents. By integrating occupational therapy (OT) assessment into resident onboarding, the evaluation identifies individual strengths and potential improvement opportunities before training. This approach aims to assist with proactive strength development, wellness, and sustainable surgical performance. Description/methods To enhance early technical skill acquisition and ergonomic awareness, our general surgery residency integrated a structured OT upper extremity and hand functional assessment prior to onboarding. Each incoming intern underwent evaluation of ergonomic health, fine motor coordination, hand strength, dexterity, and peripheral neurological status. Residents received individualized reports with suggestions for exercises to maximize performance, promoting early awareness of hand ergonomics and strategies to reduce the learning curve in surgical skill development. Results Across 2 intern cohorts from 2024 to 2025 (n = 8), residents completed a follow-up survey 4 months into training, assessing the perceived value of the OT assessment using a 5-point Likert scale. They rated the experience highly, finding it helpful for residency preparation (mean 4.5 ± 0.5), useful during training (4.0 ± 0.8), positively impactful in the operating room (3.75 ± 0.9), and worth their time (4.9 ± 0.4); 75% implemented OT recommendations and 25% pursued additional follow-up. Feedback emphasized improved ergonomic awareness, confidence, and intentional self-improvement early in training. Conclusions This project introduces an innovative, interdisciplinary approach to surgical ergonomic awareness by pairing OT expertise with resident technical development. The assessment encourages residents to consider their individual musculoskeletal strengths and ergonomic habits from the outset of training. Early integration of hand and upper-extremity assessment fosters technical readiness, enhances wellness, and may reduce overuse injuries throughout surgical residency. Potential barriers include limited OT staffing, time constraints, and cost for larger programs, which can be mitigated through streamlined protocols and involvement of OT trainees. Scheduling assessments before orientation avoids disruption to clinical duties and enhances feasibility across diverse surgical training programs. This baseline upper extremity and hand assessment was easily implemented at our institution and can be scaled to other programs with OT partnerships using standardized templates for consistent feedback and reproducibility. Minimal cost and scheduled evaluation time make it adaptable to diverse training settings.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: The open AI-native stack on Kubernetes: From open models to distributed inference and agents
piezas.resumenOriginal:
Over the past decade, Kubernetes established itself as the standard for orchestrating microservices and containerized applications. Today, we're witnessing the next major architectural shift in distributed computing: AI workloads moving from isolated research prototypes into large-scale, multi-tenant production fleets . In this post, we'll walk through the open-source stack that powers this shift and show you the sample manifests that you can try on your own Kubernetes clusters. You can also join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 to see these projects in action through live demos and technical sessions. For modern engineering teams, production AI is rapidly moving beyond generic calls to closed, black-box APIs. Organizations are realizing that their long-term competitive advantage lies in domain specialization. Platform engineers, ML researchers, and AI builders want the autonomy to run high-performing open-weight models (such as the Gemma family). They want to adapt them to proprietary enterprise datasets by using reinforcement learning (RL) and serve them with predictable latency, high throughput, and maximum hardware efficiency. Whether it's scientific initiatives training domain models like DolphinGemma (an LLM helping scientists study how dolphins communicate) on acoustic data, legal platforms evaluating complex contracts, or engineering teams building autonomous coding agents, the objective is the same: achieving frontier-level task performance at a fraction of the serving cost and latency. Yet, scaling RL post-training, stateful distributed inference, and autonomous agent execution on traditional container infrastructure introduces substantial hurdles: Accelerator underutilization in RL : When you alternate between training and rollout generation, expensive GPUs and TPUs remain idle for most of the training run. Cache-blind load balancing : When you use standard Kubernetes round-robin and least-connections routing, multi-turn agent calls are scattered across arbitrary pods and wipe out key-value (KV) cache locality. Framework fragmentation : When you operate parallel, siloed compute clusters (such as bespoke Ray or Slurm setups) alongside Kubernetes, you fragment capacity and multiply maintenance toil. Agent security in multi-tenant clusters: When you execute untrusted, model-generated shell commands and scripts in shared environments, you expose clusters to sandbox escapes and privilege escalation. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 , Google Cloud is addressing these challenges by introducing and expanding a unified, open-source AI-native stack across Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) based on these components: OpenRL (CNCF Sandbox): A Kubernetes-native post training service that simplifies RL post-training and maximizes accelerator utilization. llm-d 1.0 (CNCF Sandbox): An open distributed inference control plane that provides prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and multi-tier KV cache management. Ray on GKE with KubeRay (CNCF Sandbox) : A framework that provides enterprise lifecycle management, elastic autoscaling, and Kueue -driven scheduling for distributed Ray compute and data processing. Agent Substrate (CNCF Sandbox) : An open orchestration runtime that provides lifecycle management and execution targets for multi-turn AI agent workflows. gVisor (CNCF Sandbox) : A kernel-level container sandbox that delivers strong system call isolation when you execute untrusted agent code in multi-tenant clusters. TorchTPU : A backend that provides first-class, native PyTorch support across Cloud TPUs and GPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang . Bridge reinforcement learning and Kubernetes with OpenRL While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice, domain excellence especially in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and autonomous tool use requires RL. Historically, it's been difficult to bridge the world of ML experimentation with production Kubernetes fleets. ML researchers want to iterate rapidly in Python and PyTorch by using standard reward functions, while platform teams need multi-tenant governance, quota enforcement, and predictable scheduling. To eliminate this friction, Google created OpenRL and contributed it to the CNCF Sandbox . Architectural highlights of OpenRL Clean 4-primitive Python abstraction : Researchers write standard Python training code that's centered around four core primitives ( forward_backward , optim_step , sample , and save_state ). OpenRL translates these primitives into Kubernetes scheduling workflows without requiring developers to learn Kubernetes internals or manage infrastructure code. Cooperative accelerator time-slicing : OpenRL interleaves training steps and rollout inferences on the same physical accelerators. This approach avoids the need to dedicate separate, static clusters to compute-bound training and latency-sensitive rollout generation. Delta-weight synchronization : Shipping full multi-gigabyte model weights over cluster networking after every optimization step creates massive network saturation. OpenRL transmits only parameter deltas to rollout workers, eliminating rollout cold starts. Zero-config dynamic resource allocation ( DRA ) : OpenRL automatically profiles model context lengths, batch dimensions, and LoRA versus full fine-tuning configurations. It then dynamically bin-packs workloads across a heterogenous accelerator fleet by using native Kubernetes DRA claims. Distributed inference at scale with llm-d 1.0 After you post-train a model, serving it serving it under interactive, bursty agent traffic presents a new set of distributed systems challenges. Standard ingress controllers treat LLM traffic as stateless HTTP requests, scattering sequential turns across different replicas and constantly rebuilding KV cache. Google Cloud, Red Hat, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA co-founded the project, with contributions from over 500 engineers across 25+ organizations. Today, llm-d 1.0 is the CNCF Sandbox distributed inference control plane that transforms standalone inference engines (like vLLM and SGLang) into a coordinated, cluster-wide serving fabric. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: inference.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1

 # Routes multi-turn requests to replicas holding matching KV context

The Endpoint Picker evaluates real-time KV cache residency across worker pods. In production deployments, it's doubled KV cache hit rates from 35% to 70% and cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 70-85% on multi-turn agent workloads. 3-Tier KV cache offload : When accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) nears capacity during long-context interactions, llm-d cascades KV cache blocks from HBM → host CPU RAM → local NVMe SSD / Google Cloud Managed Lustre / Cloud Storage. This offload prevents expensive context recalculations. EPD Disaggregation with DisaggregatedSet : Decouples Encoding, Prefill, and Decode (EPD) onto specialized hardware pools that are connected by high-speed interconnects. DisaggregatedSet is built built on Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) . It enables independent horizontal scaling and coordinated, zero-downtime rolling upgrades. Native TorchTPU upstream support : PyTorch models run natively on Google Cloud TPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang through TorchTPU. Developers get day-zero parity across TPU v5e, v6e, and v7x alongside NVIDIA GPUs without the need to maintain private forks or rewrite pipelines. Latency-tolerant async processing & flow control : The llm-d-async-processor component pulls background, latency-tolerant tasks from Pub/Sub or Redis into cluster slack capacity. It applies strict traffic prioritization so background processing never degrades interactive user experiences. Fleet observability with Prism : Track cluster-wide throughput, inter-token latency (ITL), TTFT, and cache hit ratios by using Prism , the llm-d open-source benchmarking and performance dashboard. Distributed Python & ML orchestration with KubeRay While specialized runtimes handle inference and RL loops, distributed data preparation, embedding generation, and distributed PyTorch training depend heavily on Ray . KubeRay provides an open-source, Kubernetes-native operator that manages the complete lifecycle of Ray clusters, jobs, and services ( RayCluster , RayJob , and RayService custom resources) on Kubernetes. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: ray.io/v1

Native Kueue queueing & multi-tenancy : KubeRay integrates directly with Kueue for multi-tenant fair sharing, priority preemption, and quota management across shared GPU and TPU capacity. Elastic autoscaling : KubeRay dynamically scales worker pods based on active Ray tasks and actor placement, preventing idle resource consumption. Strong isolation for AI agents: Agent Substrate & gVisor As multi-turn AI agents advance from conversational assistants to autonomous systems that generate code, execute shell commands, and orchestrate external APIs running untrusted, model-generated code in shared clusters introduces serious security risks. Google Cloud is contributing Agent Substrate and continuing core contributions to gVisor in the CNCF Sandbox: Kernel-level sandboxing : gVisor provides a user-space kernel that intercepts and virtualizes system calls, which helps ensure that untrusted agent code can't compromise the host kernel or access neighboring tenant workloads. Sub-second ephemeral execution : Sandboxes spin up in milliseconds per agent turn, providing isolated execution environments for both RL rollout generation in OpenRL and live production agent workflows. Proven in practice: Mastering domain reasoning To evaluate this complete open-source stack on a rigorous enterprise workload, we tested Gemma 4 against the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) developed by Harvey.ai . This benchmark spans 24 complex legal practice areas from mergers and acquisitions (M&A)M&A due diligence to contract dispute analysis. The evaluation produced these results: Benchmark results : While standard SFT plateaued around 50% accuracy on multi-step reasoning rubrics, when we applied reproducible RL loops with OpenRL, we lifted model accuracy to 70% . Operational efficiency : The entire training pipeline dynamically shared GPU and TPU capacity with concurrent LoRA and inference jobs on GKE without manual partition management. piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

piezas.titulo: Crash-Proof Agents: Durable Execution for Long-Running AI Systems
piezas.resumenOriginal: Your Agent Is a Distributed System Wearing a Trench Coat Sometime this week, TrendForce reported that server CPU lead times stretched from 16-20 weeks to roughly 25-30 weeks, and the driver was not a new chatbot launch. It was agentic AI: workloads that stay alive for hours, holding state, invoking tools, orchestrating background work while a GPU does inference next door. The short interactive prompt-response session is giving way to persistent execution, and infrastructure planning is scrambling to catch up. Here is the uncomfortable part. Most agent code being written today assumes the machine it runs on will still be there in an hour. It assumes no deploy lands mid-run, no spot instance gets reclaimed, no pod gets evicted, no network partition eats an acknowledgment. Every one of those assumptions is false at scale, and we have known this for decades. The patterns that survive machine failure in distributed systems have names: write-ahead logs, checkpoints, idempotency keys , sagas. They work exactly as well for agents as they do for payment pipelines. They are just wearing different clothes.
